standard-deviation.name: Standard deviation calculator
standard-deviation.blurb: Sample or population, step by step.

p-value.name: P-value calculator
p-value.blurb: From z, t, χ² or F, and critical values.

standard-deviation.q1: How do you calculate standard deviation?
standard-deviation.a1: Find the mean, subtract it from each value, square the differences and add them up. Divide that sum by n − 1 for a sample (or n for a whole population) to get the variance, then take the square root.
standard-deviation.q2: Should I use the sample or the population standard deviation?
standard-deviation.a2: Use the sample value (n − 1) when your numbers are a sample from a larger group, which is almost always the case in research. Use the population value (n) only when you have every member of the group.
standard-deviation.q3: What is the difference between standard deviation and variance?
standard-deviation.a3: Variance is the average squared distance from the mean; the standard deviation is its square root, so it is in the same units as your data and easier to read.
standard-deviation.q4: What is the standard error of the mean?
standard-deviation.a4: The standard deviation divided by √n. It shows how much the mean itself would vary from sample to sample, and it is what confidence intervals and t-tests use.
standard-deviation.q5: What does the coefficient of variation tell me?
standard-deviation.a5: The standard deviation as a percentage of the mean. It compares spread between data on different scales, for example weights in kilograms and heights in centimetres.

sample-size.q1: How do I calculate sample size for a survey?
sample-size.a1: With Cochran's formula n₀ = z² × p(1 − p) ÷ e². At 95 % confidence (z = 1.96), a ±5 % margin and p = 50 % that gives 385 people. For a known population N, divide by 1 + (n₀ − 1) ÷ N.
sample-size.a2: n = N ÷ (1 + N × e²), with N the population and e the margin of error. For N = 1,000 and e = 5 % it gives 286. It assumes p = 50 % and ignores the confidence level, so many statisticians prefer Cochran's formula.
sample-size.q3: Why use 50 % as the expected proportion?
sample-size.a3: p(1 − p) is largest at 50 %, so it gives the safest (largest) sample when you do not know the answer in advance. If an earlier study found 20 %, using it gives a smaller sample.
sample-size.q4: What is the finite population correction?
sample-size.a4: When the sample is a noticeable share of a small population, fewer people are needed. Enter the population size and the calculator applies n = n₀ ÷ (1 + (n₀ − 1) ÷ N).
sample-size.q5: How many people should I invite?
sample-size.a5: Divide the sample size by the share you expect to answer. With 385 needed and a 40 % response rate, invite 963. Enter the response rate to see it.

cronbach-alpha.a1: A measure of internal consistency: how closely the items of a scale or questionnaire hang together. α = k ÷ (k − 1) × (1 − Σ item variances ÷ variance of the total score), with k the number of items.
cronbach-alpha.q2: What is a good Cronbach's alpha?
cronbach-alpha.a2: A common rule of thumb (George & Mallery, 2003): ≥ 0.9 excellent, ≥ 0.8 good, ≥ 0.7 acceptable, ≥ 0.6 questionable, ≥ 0.5 poor, below 0.5 unacceptable. Above about 0.95 the items may be redundant.
cronbach-alpha.q3: How do I paste my data?
cronbach-alpha.a3: One respondent per row and one item per column, as in Excel, Google Sheets or SPSS. Copy the cells and paste them; a header row with item names is optional. Rows with a missing score are left out.
cronbach-alpha.q4: What does alpha if item deleted mean?
cronbach-alpha.a4: The alpha the scale would have without that item. If it is higher than the current alpha (marked ↑), the item may not fit the scale or may be reverse-worded and not yet recoded.
cronbach-alpha.a5: Usually because some items are reverse-worded: agreeing with them means the opposite of the others. Recode them (for a 1–5 scale, 6 minus the score) and paste the data again.

t-test.a1: A one-sample test compares one group's mean with a fixed value. An independent samples test compares two separate groups. A paired test compares two measurements of the same people, such as before and after.
t-test.a2: Welch's test does not assume the two groups have equal variances and is the safer default, which is why it is selected first. Student's pooled test assumes equal variances and gives a whole-number df.
t-test.q3: How do I read the p-value?
t-test.a3: It is the chance of a difference at least this large if there were no real difference. Below your significance level (often 0.05), the difference is called statistically significant.
t-test.a4: The size of the difference in standard deviations. Around 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. Unlike the p-value it does not grow with the sample size.
t-test.q5: How do I report a t-test in APA style?
t-test.a5: Give t with its degrees of freedom, the p-value and an effect size, for example t(14) = 1.87, p = .082, d = 0.94. The calculator writes this line for you.

chi-square.q1: What does a chi-square test of independence tell me?
chi-square.a1: Whether two categorical variables are related, for example gender and preferred product. It compares the counts in your table with the counts expected if the variables were unrelated.
chi-square.a2: Each expected count is row total × column total ÷ grand total. χ² adds (observed − expected)² ÷ expected over every cell, with (rows − 1) × (columns − 1) degrees of freedom.
chi-square.a3: It checks whether counts in one variable match expected shares, such as a fair die (all equal) or a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. Choose Custom shares to type the expected proportions or counts.
chi-square.q4: When is a chi-square test not valid?
chi-square.a4: When expected counts are small: as a rule, no more than 20 % of cells below 5 and none below 1. The calculator warns you; for small 2 × 2 tables use Fisher's exact test instead.
chi-square.a5: An effect size for the strength of the relationship, from 0 (none) to 1 (perfect). It is √(χ² ÷ (N × (smaller of rows, columns − 1))).

p-value.q1: How do I get a p-value from a test statistic?
p-value.a1: Choose the distribution your test uses (z, t, chi-square or F), type the statistic and its degrees of freedom, and pick one or two tails. The p-value is the area of the curve beyond your statistic.
p-value.a2: Two-tailed tests a difference in either direction and is the usual choice. Use one tail only when you said in advance that only one direction counts. Chi-square and F tests are right-tailed.
p-value.a3: The cut-off your statistic must pass to be significant at level α. For a two-tailed z-test at α = 0.05 it is ± 1.96; for t it depends on the degrees of freedom.
p-value.a4: 0.05 is a convention, not a law. Some fields use 0.01 or 0.005, and a small p-value says nothing about how large or important an effect is; report an effect size too.
p-value.q5: Which degrees of freedom do I enter?
p-value.a5: One-sample or paired t: n − 1. Student's two-sample t: n₁ + n₂ − 2. Chi-square independence: (rows − 1)(columns − 1). F in a one-way ANOVA: groups − 1 and N − groups.

z-score.q1: How do you calculate a z-score?
z-score.a1: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ: subtract the mean from the value and divide by the standard deviation. An IQ of 130 with mean 100 and SD 15 has z = 2.
z-score.a2: How many standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean. About 68 % of a normal distribution lies within ± 1, 95 % within ± 1.96 and 99.7 % within ± 3.
z-score.q3: How do I turn a z-score into a percentile?
z-score.a3: The percentile is the share of the normal curve below z. z = 1 is about the 84th percentile and z = −1 the 16th. The calculator shows it as Below.
z-score.q4: How do I find the value at a percentile?
z-score.a4: Choose Percentile → value, type the percentile, the mean and the standard deviation. For example the 90th percentile of N(100, 15) is about 119.2.
z-score.q5: Do my data have to be normal?
z-score.a5: The percentages assume a normal distribution. A z-score itself is just a distance in standard deviations, but its percentile is only accurate when the data are roughly bell-shaped.

standard-deviation.lead: Find the standard deviation in three steps.
standard-deviation.s1b: Type or paste values separated by spaces, commas or new lines, or a column from a spreadsheet.
standard-deviation.s2b: Sample (n − 1) for data from a larger group, population (n) when you have every value.
standard-deviation.s3b: See the standard deviation, variance, mean and standard error, the filled-in formula and each step in the table.

sample-size.lead: Work out a survey sample size in three steps.
sample-size.s1b: Cochran for a proportion, Slovin's formula, or a mean with a known standard deviation.
sample-size.s2b: Pick the confidence level and margin of error, and add the population size and expected response rate if you know them.
sample-size.s3b: The sample size is rounded up, with the formula worked out and a table for other margins.

cronbach-alpha.lead: Check a scale's reliability in three steps.
cronbach-alpha.s1b: Select the item columns in Excel, Sheets or SPSS: one row per respondent, with or without a header.
cronbach-alpha.s2b: Paste into the box. Alpha, standardized alpha and the item table update as you type.
cronbach-alpha.s3b: Look for low item-total correlations or a higher alpha if item deleted (↑), then copy the APA line.

t-test.lead: Run a t-test in three steps.
t-test.s1b: One-sample, independent samples (Welch or Student) or paired.
t-test.s2b: Paste each group's numbers, or the before and after values in the same order.
t-test.s3b: See t, df, the p-value, the confidence interval and Cohen's d, then copy the APA-style line.

chi-square.lead: Run a chi-square test in three steps.
chi-square.s1b: Independence for a table of two variables, or goodness of fit for one variable against expected shares.
chi-square.s2b: Set the number of rows and columns (or categories) and type the observed counts.
chi-square.s3b: See χ², df, the p-value, Cramér's V and the expected counts, with a warning when they are too small.

p-value.lead: Find a p-value or critical value in three steps.
p-value.s1b: z, t, chi-square or F, the one your test statistic follows.
p-value.s2b: Type the statistic (or the significance level α for a critical value) and the degrees of freedom, and pick the tail.
p-value.s3b: The p-value with how it compares with 0.1, 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001, or the critical value and when to reject.

z-score.lead: Work with z-scores in three steps.
z-score.s1b: The z-score of a value, the value at a percentile, or the probability between two values.
z-score.s2b: Type the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ); leave 0 and 1 for the standard normal.
z-score.s3b: See z, the share below and above, and the area shaded on the bell curve.

stdDev.title: Standard deviation calculator
stdDev.privacyNote: Sample or population standard deviation, variance and standard error, worked out step by step. Your numbers stay in this tab.
stdDev.inputHint: Separate numbers with spaces, semicolons or new lines (commas too when the decimal mark is a dot), or paste a spreadsheet column.
stdDev.skipped: Skipped {n} entries that are not numbers: {list}
stdDev.truncated: Only the first {max} numbers are used.
stdDev.needTwo: A sample needs at least two numbers. Choose Population for a single value.
stdDev.stepsMore: First {n} of {total} values shown; the totals use them all.

sampleSize.title: Sample size calculator
sampleSize.privacyNote: How many people you need for a survey or study: Cochran's formula, Slovin's formula or a mean.
sampleSize.marginUnits: Margin of error (in your data's units)
sampleSize.popPlaceholder: Leave empty if large or unknown
sampleSize.hint: Not sure of the proportion? Keep 50 %: it gives the largest, safest sample.
sampleSize.needPopulation: Slovin's formula needs the population size.
sampleSize.invalid: Check the values: margin and proportion between 0 and 100, a whole-number population above zero, a response rate up to 100 %.
sampleSize.tableTitle: Sample size by margin of error

cronbach.title: Cronbach's alpha calculator
cronbach.privacyNote: Paste item scores to check a scale's internal consistency. The data stay in this tab.
cronbach.inputHint: Paste from Excel, Google Sheets or SPSS. Columns split on tabs, semicolons, commas or spaces; a first row with item names is optional.
cronbach.empty: Paste at least two rows and two item columns.
cronbach.noVariance: The total scores do not vary, so alpha cannot be computed.
cronbach.negative: Alpha is negative: some items are probably reverse-worded. Recode them and paste the data again.
cronbach.apa: APA style: Cronbach's α = {a} ({k} items, n = {n}).
cronbach.itemsHint: ↑ marks items whose removal would raise alpha. Item-total correlations below about 0.3 are often reviewed.
cronbach.truncated: Only the first {rows} respondents and {items} items are used.

tTest.title: T-test calculator
tTest.privacyNote: One-sample, independent samples or paired t-test from raw data, with an APA-style line. The data stay in this tab.
tTest.inputHint: Separate numbers with spaces, semicolons or new lines (commas too when the decimal mark is a dot). For a paired test, list both measurements in the same order.
tTest.invalid: Each group needs at least two numbers that are not all the same.
tTest.pairMismatch: A paired test needs the same number of values in both lists ({a} and {b}).
tTest.significant: Significant at α = {alpha}: the difference is unlikely to be chance alone.
tTest.curveLabel: t distribution with the p-value area shaded beyond t = {t} (p = {p})
tTest.skipped: Skipped {n} entries that are not numbers: {list}
tTest.pairSkipped: A paired test needs every entry to be a number: a skipped entry would shift the pairs. Fix or remove it in both lists.
tTest.truncated: Only the first {max} numbers are used.

chiSquare.title: Chi-square calculator
chiSquare.privacyNote: Test of independence for a contingency table, or goodness of fit for one variable. The counts stay in this tab.
chiSquare.hint: Enter counts (how many), not percentages. Custom shares can be proportions (0.5, 0.25 …), ratios (9 3 3 1) or expected counts.
chiSquare.invalid: Fill every cell with a whole-number count of zero or more; every row and column needs a total above zero.
chiSquare.lowExpected: {share} % of expected counts are below 5 (smallest {min}): the chi-square result may be unreliable. For a small 2 × 2 table, use Fisher's exact test.
chiSquare.sharesInvalid: Every expected share must be a number above zero.

pValue.title: P-value calculator
pValue.privacyNote: P-values from a z, t, chi-square or F statistic, and critical values for a significance level.
pValue.hint: Chi-square and F tests are right-tailed. Degrees of freedom may be decimals (Welch's t-test).
pValue.invalid: Enter a statistic (χ² and F zero or more), degrees of freedom above zero and up to 1,000,000, and α between 0 and 1.
pValue.curveLabel: Curve with the p-value area shaded (p = {p})

zScore.title: Z-score calculator
zScore.privacyNote: Z-scores, percentiles and probabilities under the normal curve.
zScore.hint: Use mean 0 and standard deviation 1 to work with the standard normal distribution.
zScore.invalid: Enter numbers, a standard deviation above zero and a percentile between 0 and 100.
zScore.curveBetween: Normal curve shaded between the two values ({p})
